pages.text:
QUANTITATIVE ANALYSIS OF THE SILENT
PERIOD IN THE STIFF-PERSON SYNDROME
A. J. Shatzel; G. Fenton; R. A. Maselli
(Sacramento, CA)
Introduction: The electrodiagnostic features of the stiffperson syndrome are incompletely characterized.
Objective: To define the electrodiagnostic features of the
stiff-person syndrome.
Methods: Electrodiagnostic study with measurement of the
onset of electromyographic (EMG) activity following the H
reflex in the tibial and femoral nerves.
Results: The authors studied a 68-year-old man who had a
14-year history of intermittent painful muscle contractions,
which started in his neck and progressed to involve his
extremities and trunk. In recent years, the muscle stiffness
has caused him to have recurrent falls. He was recently
diagnosed with type II diabetes. His neurologic examination
was essentially normal except for mild hypertrophy of
muscles of the lower extremities, diminished ankle jerk
reflexes, and the presence of painful muscle contractions
triggered by movements of the limbs and trunk. His
glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD) antibodies were
markedly elevated at 219 nmol/L. The electrodiagnostic
study showed normal motor and sensory conduction
velocities and normal needle EMG. However, during muscle
activation, the onset of EMG activity after the tibial H reflex
was markedly shortened in comparison with that of five
controls (10. 8+6. 5 ms, n=8 vs. 66. 8430 ms, n=22; p<0. 001).
The patient’s silent period following the femoral nerve H
reflex was also partially obliterated.
Conclusions: Quantitative analysis of the silent period
following the H reflex provides a simple methodology to
confirm the impairment of recurrent GABA-dependent
inhibitory pathways in the stiff-person syndrome.
